**Status Summary** 1. **Snapshot taken** – a full dev‑environment snapshot was created (`pre‑plugin‑incompatibility‑snapshot`) before any changes were made. 2. **Site health check** – Fetching the front‑end (`/`) and the login page (`/wp‑admin/`) both returned **HTTP 200** and displayed normal content. The fatal error you’re seeing is therefore occurring inside the admin dashboard (most likely when the plugin is loaded after login). **Root cause (based on the error you described)** The **Limit Login Attempts Reloaded** plugin is not compatible with PHP 8.3. When the dev site was upgraded to PHP 8.3, the plugin attempted to run code that uses functions/classes removed or changed in PHP 8.3, resulting in a fatal error that blocks admin access. **Policy note** – According to our operational rules, **we do not deactivate plugins or make compatibility fixes directly**. Instead we must report the incompatibility and provide a clear change plan for production. --- ## Production Change Plan | Step | Action | Reason | |------|--------|--------| | **1. Verify current production state** | Confirm the current PHP version on production (likely 8.2 or earlier) and that the site is running without errors. | Ensures we have a stable baseline before any changes. | | **2. Take a production snapshot** | Run a full file + database snapshot of the production environment (`prod‑pre‑php‑upgrade‑snapshot`). | Guarantees a roll‑back point if anything goes wrong. | | **3. Check for plugin updates** | Look for a newer release of **Limit Login Attempts Reloaded** that explicitly states compatibility with PHP 8.3 (or at least PHP 8.2+). | Updating the plugin may resolve the incompatibility without altering PHP. | | **4. Test the updated plugin on dev** | • If an update exists, install it on the **dev** site (still on PHP 8.3).
• Run a full functional check (front‑end, admin dashboard, login, any custom functionality). | Confirms the fix works before touching production. | | **5. If no compatible update exists** | • **Option A:** Keep production on the current PHP version (e.g., 8.2) until the plugin author releases a compatible version.
• **Option B:** Replace the plugin with an alternative that offers the same rate‑limiting functionality and is PHP 8.3‑ready. | Avoids a fatal error on production while maintaining security. | | **6. Apply the chosen solution to production** | • If an updated plugin was tested successfully, install it on production.
• If staying on the older PHP version, downgrade production PHP back to the previous stable version (e.g., 8.2).
• If switching plugins, deactivate **Limit Login Attempts Reloaded** (only after the alternative is active and tested) and install the replacement. | Implements the safe, tested change. | | **7. Post‑deployment verification** | • Visit the site’s front‑end (expect HTTP 200).
• Log in to the admin dashboard to confirm no fatal error.
• Test login attempts to ensure rate‑limiting works. | Guarantees the site is fully functional. | | **8. Documentation & monitoring** | Record the exact PHP version, plugin version, and any configuration changes. Set up monitoring (e.g., error‑log alerts) for the next 48 hours. | Provides traceability and early detection of regressions. | --- ### Immediate Recommendation for Production (your next manual step) - **Do not upgrade production to PHP 8.3 yet** until the **Limit Login Attempts Reloaded** plugin is verified as compatible (via an official update or replacement). - **Either** keep the current PHP version on production **or** schedule a plugin update after confirming a compatible release on dev. --- **Next actions for you (or the responsible admin):** 1. Check the plugin’s changelog on WordPress.org or the developer’s site for a PHP 8.3‑compatible version. 2. If an update exists, follow steps 3–8 above; if not, decide whether to stay on the current PHP version or replace the plugin. Feel free to let me know once you’ve identified the plugin update status, and I can help you verify the fix on the dev environment before you apply anything to production.
